title.en: Il, lo, la, i, gli, le: choosing 'the'

summary.en: Italian picks 'the' according to both gender and the first sound of the next word.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1 and 2.

Around the Locanda del Tiglio you hear *la camera*, *il campanello*, and *l'acqua calda*, yet Cesare asks for *lo scontrino* and Bruno points out *gli asciugamani* and *gli ospiti*. Every one of those small words means 'the'.

| Gender & starting sound | Singular | Plural | Indefinite ('a / an') |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Feminine before a consonant | *la chiave* | *le chiavi* | *una camera* |
| Feminine before a vowel | *l'acqua* | *le ore* | *un'ora* |
| Masculine before most consonants | *il campanello* | *i panini* | *un tavolo* |
| Masculine before `s` + consonant, `z`, `gn`, `ps` | *lo scontrino* | *gli specchi* | *uno specchio* |
| Masculine before a vowel | *l'albergo* | *gli ospiti* | *un ospite* |

Learn each noun together with its article—hearing *lo scontrino* or *la chiave* as a single rhythmic unit tells you both the noun's gender and how its plural will behave.

On replay, notice how smoothly `l'` links directly onto vowel-initial nouns like *l'acqua*, while *lo* adds a clear vowel cushion before *scontrino*.
